newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa worried by apparent religious bomb attacks.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa worried by apparent religious bomb attacks.

text.p: South African police appealed for calm on Monday in the wake of bomb attacks that appeared to signal a white right-wing campaign of violence against Moslems.
A previously unknown extreme-right group has claimed responsibility for the attacks in the name of Christianity.

"Although fully aware of the extreme provocation of bombing a mosque and centre of learning, I must appeal for calm from the affected community," acting police commissioner Zoli Lavisa said after a weekend blast injured two at a mosque.
"Any over-reaction, verbal or physical, could spark a new spiral of counter-violence which would play into the hands of the extremists responsible for these latest bomb outrages."

Police minister Sydney Mufamadi, referring to white right-wingers who opposed South Africa's transition from racial oppression to democracy, said the bombers must be "racial bigots who have a propensity for the old order".

A telephone caller claiming to represent the right-wing Boere Attack Troops (BAT), a previously unknown group, told state television it was responsible for the weekend bombings near Johannesburg as well as two explosions near Cape Town on Christmas Eve.
Four people were killed and dozens injured by the two pipe bombs which exploded in the town of Worcester northeast of Cape Town on December 24.
The telephone caller told the broadcaster his group was opposed to Moslems because they rejected Christianity.
The man claimed to recognise Nelson Mandela as president and blacks as indigenous South Africans, but wanted all Indians thrown out of parliament.
The head of the Moslem Judicial Council, Nazeem Mohammed, told state radio the council planned strong action in reply to the attack and Moslem groups would meet on Monday for talks.

Among those expected to take part in the discussions is a controversial Moslem vigilante group -- People Against Gangsterism and Drugs (Pagad) -- which carried out fire-bomb and grenade attacks on the homes of alleged drug dealers.

Pagad gained prominence in August when supporters publicly shot and burned to death an alleged drug-baron, and since then members have clashed several times with police over their violent campaign against suspected criminals.
Police arrested two white mineworkers on Sunday after the three blasts in and around the conservative platinum mining town of Rustenburg in North West province.
The two later appeared in court where they were refused bail and ordered to appear again on January 10.
Explosives were allegedly found in the car they were driving and at one of the men's homes, a police spokeswoman said.

Hardline right-wingers such as Afrikaner Resistance Movement (AWB) leader Eugene Terre Blanche issued frequent warnings of civil war ahead of the 1994 election, demanding self-rule for Afrikaners, but their potential to cause serious disruption had appeared to dissipate since the country's all-race polls.
Terre Blanche has said his group did not carry out the attacks, but "understood the degree of frustration" of right-wingers.

Robert van Tonder, leader of the tiny separatist Boerestaat Party, said his group had no knowledge or link to the BAT, but believed that South Africa's non-racial constitution had made the ballot-box irrelevant.
The Boers, descendants of Dutch and French settlers from over three centuries ago, would only regain their freedom through struggle, van Tonder said in a statement.
